Good on the Aussies 👍👍👍👍👍 

Five members of Iran's women's national football team have been granted humanitarian visas (effectively asylum/refuge) in Australia as of March 9, 2026. This follows their participation in the Women's Asian Cup on the Gold Coast, where the team was eliminated after a loss to the Philippines.
The players named in multiple credible sources (including statements from Australia's Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, and Prince Reza Pahlavi's communications office) are:

Fatemeh Pasandideh
Zahra Ghanbari
Zahra Sarbali
Atefeh Ramazanzadeh
Mona Hamoudi

They reportedly left the team's hotel (with some assistance from Australian Federal Police), sought protection, and were moved to a safe location before their visas were processed and granted. This came amid heightened fears for their safety due to political tensions, including the ongoing regional conflict involving Iran, and backlash in Iran over the team not singing the national anthem during a match (viewed by some hardliners as a protest or disloyalty, labelling them "traitors").

Recent photos shared publicly (including by Australian officials meeting the players and on social media from supporters) show these women without hijabs, appearing in casual or team-related attire in a relaxed setting in Australia. This contrasts with images of the team during the tournament, where compulsory hijab rules under Iran's regime would typically apply for public appearances. The removal aligns with their new environment in Australia, where such mandates don't exist, symbolizing a step toward personal freedom for them.
Australia's government has extended offers of safety and visa options to the remaining players on the team as well, though it's unclear how many (if any) will take it up, some reports note the coach and others expressing a desire to return home, possibly due to family pressures or other factors.

The situation highlights the severe risks faced by women athletes (and citizens) under Iran's theocratic regime, including potential punishment for perceived dissent. 
Many see this as a positive outcome for the five who have escaped to safety, while concern remains for anyone still in Iran or choosing to return. The Islamic Republic's enforcement of compulsory hijab and suppression of women's rights has long been criticized internationally as oppressive.
